Implement the single-use refresh rotation (overwrite the stored refresh token on every token response) and revocation on disconnect

approval.cost: No fee for creating or running an OAuth app is stated in the docs read
approval.trigger: No app review, approval, verification, or listing process is described anywhere in the official Calendly developer documentation read. A developer registers a Production OAuth application directly in the portal and users can authorize it; there is no Calendly-side gate, no stated pre-approval user cap, no marketplace/listing submission process for OAuth apps, and no fee stated. The gates that exist are on the USER side, not the app side: 'Developers can make GET and POST requests to API endpoints on behalf of a Calendly user on any subscription plan, including the Free plan (with the exception of a few endpoints that are specific to our Enterprise plan)', and API access in general 'is determined by your subscription and user role in Calendly'. Webhooks are the exception: 'access to webhooks is reserved for members on paid premium subscriptions and above', specifically 'the Calendly user account for which the webhook subscription is being made will need a paid subscription on the Standard, Teams, or Enterprise plan'.

blockers.detail: Calendly is moving to OAuth 2.1-style rotation: 'A refresh token is revoked immediately after a successful POST /oauth/token call', and every successful response returns a new refresh token. Your client 'Treats refresh tokens as single-use' and must 'Immediately overwrite the stored refresh token with the new refresh_token from every successful POST /oauth/token response'. Reusing an old one returns HTTP 400/401 with invalid_grant, at which point the docs tell you to clear tokens and have the user re-authorize. Parallel/concurrent refresh attempts racing on the same stored token can burn it the same way. 'The deadline for updating your refresh token behavior is August 31, 2026.'
blockers.howToClear: Serialize refreshes per user and atomically persist each new refresh token; migrate before the August 31, 2026 enforcement deadline.
blockers.title: Single-use rotating refresh tokens

blockers.detail: 'Be sure to copy these values as you will not be able to access the Client Secret or Webhook signing key again.' They are also not shown when you later edit the app. Lose them and the documented remedy is effectively a new app (the docs state no regeneration flow).
blockers.howToClear: Store both values in a secrets manager at app creation.
blockers.title: Credentials are show-once

blockers.detail: 'For newly created OAuth apps and new Personal Access Tokens, no API access is granted until scopes are explicitly requested and approved.' Users 'can decline scopes during install', so your app must cope with partial grants; 'For existing installs, you may need to reauthorize the app to request additional scopes.'
blockers.howToClear: Request the full scope set up front and handle declined scopes gracefully.
blockers.title: Scopes are opt-in and user-negotiable

Any limit on the number of users who can authorize one app, or on the number of OAuth apps per developer account (not stated).
Personal access token expiry (the PAT docs say tokens are not displayed or stored by Calendly and are 'unretrievable' after generation, but state no expiration).

alternatives: Personal Access Tokens (PATs): for internal/private apps acting on a single account only. 'OAuth is required for multiple accounts, while personal access tokens are used for installing in a single account at a time.' A PAT is generated by the account holder (Calendly account > Integrations > API & Webhooks) with scopes selected at creation and sent as a Bearer token; it is not a delegated/multi-user mechanism (except the degenerate case where each user pastes their own PAT into your product, which Calendly positions as an internal-app pattern)
flavor.recommended: A Production 'web' OAuth application using the authorization code flow with PKCE (S256), one app per environment
flavor.why: The object is an OAuth application, created in the Calendly Developer Portal under a Calendly developer account (signed up with GitHub or Google; the docs stress this 'is not your Calendly user account and is not associated with your Calendly user account'). Calendly brands its current implementation OAuth 2.1 for API v2. At creation you pick the kind of app (web or native), the environment (Sandbox or Production, separate apps), a redirect URI, and a set of scopes. Creating the app issues a Client Id, Client Secret, and Webhook signing key. 'If you need to provide a way for Calendly members to securely share their Calendly account data with a public application you've built, then use OAuth 2.1'; 'If you're integrating a public application that many Calendly users will use, authenticate with OAuth.'

humanMust: Sign up for a Calendly developer account (GitHub or Google) in the Developer Portal
Create the OAuth application (name; kind web/native; environment Sandbox or Production; redirect URI; scopes) and copy the Client Id, Client Secret, and Webhook signing key immediately
Create a second application for Production when ready to go live with customer data (Sandbox and Production are separate apps)
name: Calendly
nuances: Account changes kill tokens: both OAuth and personal access tokens 'will be revoked if: The account's login email is changed. The account's password is changed. The account's login method is changed.' Tokens can also be revoked manually (OAuth: POST to the revoke endpoint; PATs: 'Revoke' on the API & Webhooks page).

PKCE guidance is internally inconsistent: the registration procedure says 'For all OAuth applications (web or native) use a specific redirect_uri, a Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE), and S256 for code_challenge_method', but the testing section then says 'While we will not enforce PKCE for web applications, we recommend using PKCE conforming to the RFC 7636 specification for both web and native applications.' Build PKCE regardless. Sandbox allows HTTP on localhost for redirect URIs; Production must be HTTPS.

A :write scope implicitly includes the matching :read scope. Legacy (pre-scope) apps and PATs 'retain full access to available endpoints by default', and when a legacy token is refreshed it is 'automatically migrated to the scoped token format' without reauthorization.

Token endpoint exchange details: 'Web clients: pass client_id and client_secret via Basic HTTP Authorization header. Native clients: include client_id as a body param within the API call' (native clients use the PKCE code_verifier). The token response contains access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, owner (user URI), organization, and scope. The authorize URL 'must be requested using a web browser'.
prerequisites: A Calendly developer account (separate from any Calendly user account)
An HTTPS redirect URI for the Production app
Server-side token storage that overwrites the refresh token on every token response

steps.detail: Sign up with GitHub or Google in the Developer Portal (not your Calendly user account). Create a new OAuth application: name; kind (web); environment (start with Sandbox); redirect URI (Sandbox allows HTTP on localhost; Production must be HTTPS); select scopes.
steps.title: Create the OAuth application (Sandbox first)

steps.detail: 'Be sure to copy these values as you will not be able to access the Client Secret or Webhook signing key again.' When ready to go live, create a second application for Production (separate credentials).
steps.title: Copy credentials immediately; create the Production app later

steps.detail: Generate a CODE_VERIFIER and CODE_CHALLENGE (PKCE, S256). Redirect the user to auth.calendly.com/oauth/authorize?client_id=...&response_type=code&redirect_uri=...&code_challenge_method=S256&code_challenge=... (scopes can be passed space-separated in a scope parameter). The user grants access; you receive the authorization code on your redirect URI.
steps.title: Redirect the user (PKCE S256)

steps.detail: POST auth.calendly.com/oauth/token with grant_type, code, and redirect_uri. 'Access Tokens expire after 2 hours.' 'Refresh Tokens don't expire until they are used.' Token-endpoint rate limit: 'Only 8 oauth tokens per user can be requested within a span of 1 minute'.
steps.title: Exchange the code; call API v2

steps.detail: POST /oauth/token with grant_type=refresh_token, treating refresh tokens as single-use: immediately overwrite the stored refresh token with the new one from every successful response. Revoke via the documented revoke endpoint when a user disconnects.
steps.title: Refresh (single-use) and revoke

tagline: Self-service OAuth 2.1 with no app review at all: the friction is mechanical. Two-hour access tokens, refresh tokens that become single-use (enforcement deadline August 31, 2026), show-once credentials, separate Sandbox and Production apps, and webhooks gated by the end user's paid plan.

time.active: ~15 min of portal setup + ~1-2 hrs of flow code
